hints: Look closely at where the dark chromosomes are in each labelled cell. Is the chromatin a tangled ball, lined up in the middle, or pulled apart into two groups?
Remember the order of mitosis: prophase has condensing chromosomes still scattered in the nucleus, metaphase has them lined up on the equator, anaphase has sister chromatids moving to opposite poles.
walkthrough:
**Look at cell X**

Cell X shows dark, thick chromosomes as a tangled mass filling the centre. The nuclear envelope is breaking down but there is no plate and no separation.

This is the classic look of prophase, when chromosomes condense and become visible.

**Look at cell Y**

Cell Y shows the chromosomes lined up in a neat row across the middle of the cell. They are attached and waiting to be pulled apart.

Lining up on the metaphase plate (equator) defines metaphase.

**Look at cell Z**

Cell Z shows two separate groups of chromosomes moving away from each other toward opposite ends of the cell.

Separation of sister chromatids to opposite poles defines anaphase.

**Match to the table**

So anaphase is Z, metaphase is Y, prophase is X. That combination is option D.

options.A: X is not anaphase because its chromosomes are not separated into two groups, and Z is not prophase because its chromosomes are already pulled apart.
options.B: Y is not anaphase, it shows chromosomes lined up on the equator for metaphase, and Z is not metaphase, it shows separation for anaphase.
options.C: X is not metaphase because there is no equatorial plate, X is prophase with tangled condensing chromosomes, and Y is not prophase.
options.D: Correct. Z shows two groups moving to poles (anaphase), Y shows line-up on the equator (metaphase), X shows tangled condensed chromosomes (prophase).
